subsection.title: Introduction

figure.caption: The great mathematician Leonard Euler observed “… nothing at all takes place in the universe in which some rule of maximum or minimum does not appear.” In Exercise 4.7.53 you will use calculus to show that bees construct the cells in their hive in a shape that minimizes surface area.

subsection.paragraph: WE HAVE ALREADY INVESTIGATED SOME of the applications of derivatives, but now that we know the differentiation rules we are in a better position to pursue the applications of differentiation in greater depth. Here we learn what derivatives tell us about the shape of a graph of a function and, in particular, how they help us locate maximum and minimum values of functions. Many practical problems require us to minimize a cost or maximize an area or somehow find the best possible outcome of a situation. In particular, we will be able to investigate the optimal shape of a can and to explain the location of rainbows in the sky.

content.paragraph: Some of the most important applications of differential calculus are optimization problems, in which we are required to find the optimal (best) way of doing something. Here are examples of such problems that we will solve in this chapter:

item.paragraph: What is the shape of a can that minimizes manufacturing costs?
What is the maximum acceleration of a spacecraft? (This is an important question for the astronauts who have to withstand the effects of acceleration.)
What is the radius of a contracted windpipe that expels air most rapidly during a cough?
At what angle should blood vessels branch so as to minimize the energy expended by the heart in pumping blood?

content.paragraph: These problems can be reduced to finding the maximum or minimum values of a function. Let’s first explain exactly what we mean by maximum and minimum values.

subsection.title: Absolute and Local Extreme Values
subsection.paragraph: We see that the highest point on the graph of the function $$f$$ shown in Figure 1 is the point $$\left( {3,5} \right)$$ . In other words, the largest value of $$f$$ is $$f(3) = 5$$ . Likewise, the smallest value is $$f(6) = 2$$ . We say that $$f(3) = 5$$ is the absolute maximum of $$f$$ and $$f(6) = 2$$ is the absolute minimum. In general, we use the following definition.

The y axis is displayed from negative 1 to 6 in increments of 1 unit. The curve begins at the point (1, 3), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at (3, 5), goes down and to the right becoming concave up, reaches its low point at (6, 2), again goes up and ends at the point (7, 3).

note.title: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $$c$$ be a number in the domain $$D$$ of a function $$f$$ . Then $$f(c)$$ is the

item.paragraph: absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ if $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ .
absolute minimum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ if $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ .

subsection.paragraph: An absolute maximum or minimum is sometimes called a global maximum or minimum. The maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ are called extreme values of $$f$$ .

Figure 2 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ with absolute maximum at $$d$$ and absolute minimum at $$a$$ . Note that $$\left( {d,f(d)} \right)$$ is the highest point on the graph and $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ is the lowest point. In Figure 2, if we consider only values of $$x$$ near $$b$$ [for instance, if we restrict our attention to the interval $$\left( {a,c} \right)$$ ], then $$f(b)$$ is the largest of those values of $$f(x)$$ and is called a local maximum value of $$f$$ . Likewise, $$f(c)$$ is called a local minimum value of $$f$$ because $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ for $$x$$ near $$c$$ [in the interval $$\left( {b,d} \right)$$ , for instance]. The function $$f$$ also has a local minimum at $$e$$ . In general, we have the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.paragraph: The number $$f(c)$$ is a

item.paragraph: local maximum value of $$f$$ if $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ when $$x$$ is near $$c$$ .
local minimum value of $$f$$ if $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ when $$x$$ is near $$c$$ .

subsection.paragraph: In Definition 2 (and elsewhere), if we say that something is true near $$c$$ , we mean that it is true on some open interval containing $$c$$ . (Thus a local maximum or minimum can’t occur at an endpoint.) For instance, in Figure 3 we see that $$f(4) = 5$$ is a local minimum because it’s the smallest value of $$f$$ on the interval $$I$$ . It’s not the absolute minimum because $$f(x)$$ takes on smaller values when $$x$$ is near $$12$$ (in the interval $$K$$ , for instance). In fact $$f(12) = 3$$ is both a local minimum and the absolute minimum. Similarly, $$f(8) = 7$$ is a local maximum, but not the absolute maximum because $$f$$ takes on larger values near $$1$$ .

However, there is no highest point on the parabola and so this function has no maximum value.

subsection.paragraph: We have seen that some functions have extreme values, whereas others do not. The following theorem gives conditions under which a function is guaranteed to possess extreme values.

note.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ attains an absolute maximum value $$f(c)$$ and an absolute minimum value $$f(d)$$ at some numbers $$c$$ and $$d$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

subsection.paragraph: The Extreme Value Theorem is illustrated in Figure 8. Note that an extreme value can be taken on more than once. Although the Extreme Value Theorem is intuitively very plausible, it is difficult to prove and so we omit the proof.

figure.caption: Functions continuous on a closed interval always attain extreme values.

subsection.paragraph: The function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 9 is defined on the closed interval $$\lbrack 0,2\rbrack$$ but has no maximum value. (Notice that the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack 0,3)$$ . The function takes on values arbitrarily close to $$3$$ , but never actually attains the value $$3$$ .) This does not contradict the Extreme Value Theorem because $$f$$ is not continuous. [Nonetheless, a discontinuous function could have maximum and minimum values. See Exercise 13(b).]

The function $$g$$ shown in Figure 10 is continuous on the open interval $$(0,2)$$ but has neither a maximum nor a minimum value. [The range of $$g$$ is $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ . The function takes on arbitrarily large values.] This does not contradict the Extreme Value Theorem because the interval $$(0,2)$$ is not closed.

subsection.title: Critical Numbers and the Closed Interval Method
subsection.paragraph: The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed interval has a maximum value and a minimum value, but it does not tell us how to find these extreme values. Notice in Figure 8 that the absolute maximum and minimum values that are between $$a$$ and $$b$$ occur at local maximum or minimum values, so we start by looking for local extreme values.

Figure 11 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ with a local maximum at $$c$$ and a local minimum at $$d$$ . It appears that at the maximum and minimum points the tangent lines are horizontal and therefore each has slope $$0$$ . We know that the derivative is the slope of the tangent line, so it appears that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(d) = 0$$ . The following theorem says that this is always true for differentiable functions.

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The positive x axis is displayed with tick marks c and d in the order from left to right. The curve goes up and to the right from the second quadrant, crosses the y axis, becomes concave down, and reaches its high point at x = c. This high point is labeled (c, f(c)). It then goes down and to the right, becoming concave up, reaches its low point labeled (d, f(d)), and then goes up and to the right. A horizontal tangent is drawn above the high point and touches it exactly once at (c, f(c)). Another horizontal tangent is drawn below the curve and touches it exactly once at (d, f(d)). Vertical segments from tick marks c and d reach the curve.

note.title: Fermat’s Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ , and if $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ exists, then $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .

note.title: Proof
note.paragraph: Suppose, for the sake of definiteness, that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ . Then, according to Definition 2, $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ if $$x$$ is sufficiently close to $$c$$ . This implies that if $$h$$ is sufficiently close to $$0$$ , with $$h$$ being positive or negative, then

We have shown that $$f^{\prime}(c) \geqslant 0$$ and also that $$f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant 0$$ . Since both of these inequalities must be true, the only possibility is that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .
We have proved Fermat’s Theorem for the case of a local maximum. The case of a local minimum can be proved in a similar manner, or see Exercise 81 for an alternate method.

subsection.paragraph: The following examples caution us against reading too much into Fermat’s Theorem: we can’t expect to locate extreme values simply by setting $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and solving for $$x$$ .

problem.paragraph: If $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . But $$f$$ has no maximum or minimum at $$0$$ , as you can see from its graph in Figure 12. (Or observe that $$x^{3} > 0$$ for $$x > 0$$ but $$x^{3} < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ .) The fact that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ simply means that the curve $$y = x^{3}$$ has a horizontal tangent at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Instead of having a maximum or minimum at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , the curve crosses its horizontal tangent there.

subsection.paragraph: Warning Examples 5 and 6 show that we must be careful when using Fermat’s Theorem. Example 5 demonstrates that even when $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ there need not be a maximum or minimum at $$c$$ . (In other words, the converse of Fermat’s Theorem is false in general.) Furthermore, there may be an extreme value even when $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist (as in Example 6).

Fermat’s Theorem does suggest that we should at least start looking for extreme values of $$f$$ at the numbers $$c$$ where $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or where $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist. Such numbers are given a special name.

note.title: Definition
note.paragraph: A critical number of a function $$f$$ is a number $$c$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that either $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist.

subsection.paragraph: In terms of critical numbers, Fermat’s Theorem can be rephrased as follows (compare Definition 6 with Theorem 4):

To find an absolute maximum or minimum of a continuous function on a closed interval, we note that either it is local [in which case it occurs at a critical number by (7)] or it occurs at an endpoint of the interval, as we see from the examples in Figure 8. Thus the following three-step procedure always works.

note.title: The Closed Interval Method
note.paragraph: To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function $$f$$ on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ :

item.paragraph: Find the values of $$f$$ at the critical numbers of $$f$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
Find the values of $$f$$ at the endpoints of the interval.
The largest of the values from Steps 1 and 2 is the absolute maximum value; the smallest of these values is the absolute minimum value.

statement.paragraph: Explain the difference between an absolute minimum and a local minimum.

answer.paragraph: Abs min: smallest function value on the entire domain of the function; loc min at $$c$$ : smallest function value when $$x$$ is near $$c$$

subsection.title: Applied Project The Calculus of Rainbows
subsection.paragraph: Rainbows are created when raindrops scatter sunlight. They have fascinated mankind since ancient times and have inspired attempts at scientific explanation since the time of Aristotle. In this project we use the ideas of Descartes and Newton to explain the shape, location, and colors of rainbows.

figure.caption: Formation of the primary rainbow
figure.alt_text: An illustration shows a spherical raindrop and three points are marked on the circumference of the sphere: point A at the top left of the spherical drop; point B on the right side, and point C at the bottom. From the center of the spherical drop O, three dashed lines are drawn through the points A, B, and C. On the left side of the drop, the ray from the sun travels horizontally rightward and enters the spherical drop at the labeled point A. This ray makes an angle alpha with the extended line O A. It then travels down and to the right, and intersects the drop at point B, making an angle Beta with both the dashed lines O A and O B. From point B, the ray then travels down and to the left and intersects the drop at point C. This ray B C makes an angle Beta with both the dashed lines O B and O C. The ray then extends downward outside the spherical drop, but not as steep as ray B C, thus reflecting to an observer. This extended ray from point C makes an angle alpha with the extended dashed line O C. From point A, a dashed horizontal line extends rightward. From point C, a dashed line segment extends upward along with the extended downward slanting ray, goes up and to the right of ray B C, and meets the dashed horizontal line, making an obtuse angle D(alpha).

item.paragraph: The figure shows a ray of sunlight entering a spherical raindrop at A. Some of the light is reflected, but the line AB shows the path of the part that enters the drop. Notice that the light is refracted toward the normal line AO and in fact Snell’s Law says that $$\sin\alpha = k\sin\beta$$ , where $$\alpha$$ is the angle of incidence, $$\beta$$ is the angle of refraction, and $$k \approx \frac{4}{3}$$ is the index of refraction for water. At B some of the light passes through the drop and is refracted into the air, but the line BC shows the part that is reflected. (The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.) When the ray reaches C, part of it is reflected, but for the time being we are more interested in the part that leaves the raindrop at C. (Notice that it is refracted away from the normal line.) The angle of deviation $$D(\alpha)$$ is the amount of clockwise rotation that the ray has undergone during this three-stage process. Thus
Show that the minimum value of the deviation is $$D(\alpha) \approx 138^{{^\circ}}$$ and occurs when $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ .

The significance of the minimum deviation is that when $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ we have $$D^{\prime}(\alpha) \approx 0$$ , so $$\Delta D \slash \Delta\alpha \approx 0$$ . This means that many rays with $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ become deviated by approximately the same amount. It is the concentration of rays coming from near the direction of minimum deviation that creates the brightness of the primary rainbow. The figure below shows that the angle of elevation from the observer up to the highest point on the rainbow is $$180^{{^\circ}} - 138^{{^\circ}} = 42^{{^\circ}}$$ . (This angle is called the rainbow angle.)

figure.alt_text: An illustration shows an observer on the ground on the left side and an arch-shaped rainbow on the right side with a few raindrops at its high point. A diagonal line connects the observer and the high point of the rainbow. A downward slanting ray, labeled rays from sun, passes through the observer from left to right, making an angle of 42 degrees with the diagonal line. Another downward slanting ray, labeled rays from sun, passes through the high point of the rainbow, parallel to the previous ray, making an angle of 138 degrees with the diagonal line, to the right of it. Two dashed lines from the observer connect the endpoints of the arch-shaped rainbow.

item.paragraph: Problem 1 explains the location of the primary rainbow, but how do we explain the colors? Sunlight comprises a range of wavelengths, from the red range through orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. As Newton discovered in his prism experiments of 1666, the index of refraction is different for each color. (The effect is called dispersion.) For red light the refractive index is $$k \approx 1.3318$$ , whereas for violet light it is $$k \approx 1.3435$$ . By repeating the calculation of Problem 1 for these values of $$k$$ , show that the rainbow angle is about $$42.3^{{^\circ}}$$ for the red bow and $$40.6^{{^\circ}}$$ for the violet bow. So the rainbow really consists of seven individual bows corresponding to the seven colors.

note.title: Fermat
note.paragraph: Fermat’s Theorem is named after Pierre Fermat (1601–1665), a French lawyer who took up mathematics as a hobby. Despite his amateur status, Fermat was one of the two inventors of analytic geometry (Descartes was the other). His methods for finding tangents to curves and maximum and minimum values (before the invention of limits and derivatives) made him a forerunner of Newton in the creation of differential calculus.

content.paragraph: We will see that many of the results of this chapter depend on one central fact, which is called the Mean Value Theorem.

subsection.title: Rolle’s Theorem
subsection.paragraph: To arrive at the Mean Value Theorem, we first need the following result.

note.title: Rolle’s Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function that satisfies the following three hypotheses:

item.paragraph: $$f$$ is continuous on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .
$$f$$ is differentiable on the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

note.paragraph: Then there is a number $$c$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ such that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .

note.title: Rolle
note.paragraph: Rolle’s Theorem was first published in 1691 by the French mathematician Michel Rolle (1652–1719) in a book entitled Méthode pour resoudre les egalitez. He was a vocal critic of the methods of his day and attacked calculus as being a “collection of ingenious fallacies.” Later, however, he became convinced of the essential correctness of the methods of calculus.

subsection.paragraph: Before giving the proof let’s take a look at the graphs of some typical functions that satisfy the three hypotheses. Figure 1 shows the graphs of four such functions. In each case it appears that there is at least one point $$\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ on the graph where the tangent is horizontal and therefore $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ . Thus Rolle’s Theorem is plausible.

note.title: Proof
note.paragraph: There are three cases:
Take cases
CASE I $$\mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = \mathbf{k}$$ , a constant
Then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , so the number $$c$$ can be taken to be any number in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

CASE II $$f(x) > \mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{a} \right)$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\left( {\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}} \right)$$ [as in Figure 1(b) or (c)] By the Extreme Value Theorem (which we can apply by hypothesis 1), $$f$$ has a maximum value somewhere in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Since $$f(a) = f(b)$$ , it must attain this maximum value at a number $$c$$ in the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ and, by hypothesis 2, $$f$$ is differentiable at $$c$$ . Therefore $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ by Fermat’s Theorem.

CASE III $$\mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right) < \mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{a} \right)$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\left( {\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}} \right)$$ [as in Figure 1(c) or (d)] By the Extreme Value Theorem, $$f$$ has a minimum value in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and, since $$f(a) = f(b)$$ , it attains this minimum value at a number $$c$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Again $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ by Fermat’s Theorem.

problem.paragraph: Let’s apply Rolle’s Theorem to the position function $$s = f(t)$$ of a moving object. If the object is in the same place at two different instants $$t = a$$ and $$t = b$$ , then $$f(a) = f(b)$$ . Rolle’s Theorem says that there is some instant of time $$t = c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ when $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ ; that is, the velocity is $$0$$ . (In particular, you can see that this is true when a ball is thrown directly upward.)
Prove that the equation $$x^{3} + x - 1 = 0$$ has exactly one real solution.

Solution First we use the Intermediate Value Theorem (2.5.10) to show that a solution exists. Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1$$ . Then $$f(0) = - 1 < 0$$ and $$f(1) = 1 > 0$$ . Since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is continuous, so the Intermediate Value Theorem states that there is a number $$c$$ between $$0$$ and $$1$$ such that $$f(c) = 0$$ . Thus the given equation has a solution.

To show that the equation has no other real solution, we use Rolle’s Theorem and argue by contradiction. Suppose that it had two solutions $$a$$ and $$b$$ . Then $$f(a) = 0 = f(b)$$ and, since $$f$$ is a polynomial, it is differentiable on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Thus, by Rolle’s Theorem, there is a number $$c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ such that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ . But
(since $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ ) so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ can never be $$0$$ . This gives a contradiction. Therefore the equation can’t have two real solutions.

Figure 2 shows a graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1$$ discussed in Example 2. Rolle’s Theorem shows that, no matter how much we enlarge the viewing rectangle, we can never find a second $$x$$-intercept.

subsection.title: The Mean Value Theorem
subsection.paragraph: Our main use of Rolle’s Theorem is in proving the following important theorem, which was first stated by another French mathematician, Joseph-Louis Lagrange.

note.title: The Mean Value Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function that satisfies the following hypotheses:

item.paragraph: $$f$$ is continuous on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .
$$f$$ is differentiable on the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

note.paragraph: Then there is a number $$c$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ such that
or, equivalently,

The Mean Value Theorem is an example of what is called an existence theorem. Like the Intermediate Value Theorem, the Extreme Value Theorem, and Rolle’s Theorem, it guarantees that there exists a number with a certain property, but it doesn’t tell us how to find the number.

problem.paragraph: If an object moves in a straight line with position function $$s = f(t)$$ , then the average velocity between $$t = a$$ and $$t = b$$ is

and the velocity at $$t = c$$ is $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ . Thus the Mean Value Theorem (in the form of Equation 1) tells us that at some time $$t = c$$ between $$a$$ and $$b$$ the instantaneous velocity $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ is equal to that average velocity. For instance, if a car traveled $$180$$ km in $$2$$ hours, then the speedometer must have read $$90{km} \slash h$$ at least once.
In general, the Mean Value Theorem can be interpreted as saying that there is a number at which the instantaneous rate of change is equal to the average rate of change over an interval.

subsection.paragraph: The main significance of the Mean Value Theorem is that it enables us to obtain information about a function from information about its derivative. The next example provides an instance of this principle.

note.title: Lagrange and the Mean Value Theorem
note.paragraph: The Mean Value Theorem was first formulated by Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1736–1813), born in Italy of a French father and an Italian mother. He was a child prodigy and became a professor in Turin at the age of 19. Lagrange made great contributions to number theory, theory of functions, theory of equations, and analytical and celestial mechanics. In particular, he applied calculus to the analysis of the stability of the solar system. At the invitation of Frederick the Great, he succeeded Euler at the Berlin Academy and, when Frederick died, Lagrange accepted King Louis XVI’s invitation to Paris, where he was given apartments in the Louvre and became a professor at the Ecole Polytechnique. Despite all the trappings of luxury and fame, he was a kind and quiet man, living only for science.

section.title: What Derivatives Tell Us about the Shape of a Graph

content.paragraph: Many of the applications of calculus depend on our ability to deduce facts about a function $$f$$ from information concerning its derivatives. Because $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ represents the slope of the curve $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ , it tells us the direction in which the curve proceeds at each point. So it is reasonable to expect that information about $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ will provide us with information about $$f(x)$$ .

subsection.title: What Does f ′ Say about f ?
subsection.paragraph: To see how the derivative of $$f$$ can tell us where a function is increasing or decreasing, look at Figure 1. (Increasing functions and decreasing functions were defined in Section 1.1.) Between $$A$$ and $$B$$ and between $$C$$ and $$D$$ , the tangent lines have positive slope and so $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ . Between $$B$$ and $$C$$ , the tangent lines have negative slope and so $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . Thus it appears that $$f$$ increases when $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive and decreases when $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative. To prove that this is always the case, we use the Mean Value Theorem.

problem.paragraph: Find where the function $$f(x) = 3x^{4} - 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 5$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.
Solution We start by differentiating $$f$$ :

To use the I/D Test we have to know where $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ and where $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . To solve these inequalities we first find where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , namely at $$x = 0,2,{and} - 1$$ . These are the critical numbers of $$f$$ , and they divide the domain into four intervals (see the number line Figure 2). Within each interval, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ must be always positive or always negative. (See Examples 3 and 4 in Appendix A.) We can determine which is the case for each interval from the signs of the three factors of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , namely, $$12x$$ , $$x - 2$$ , and $$x + 1$$ as shown in the following chart. A plus sign indicates that the given expression is positive, and a minus sign indicates that it is negative. The last column of the chart gives the conclusion based on the I/D Test. For instance, $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$0 < x < 2$$ , so $$f$$ is decreasing on $$(0,2)$$ . (It would also be true to say that $$f$$ is decreasing on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ .)
The graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 3 confirms the information in the chart.

subsection.title: The First Derivative Test
subsection.paragraph: Recall from Section 4.1 that if $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ , then $$c$$ must be a critical number of $$f$$ (by Fermat’s Theorem), but not every critical number gives rise to a maximum or a minimum. We therefore need a test that will tell us whether or not $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at a critical number.

You can see from Figure 3 that $$f(0) = 5$$ is a local maximum value of $$f$$ because $$f$$ increases on $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and decreases on $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ . Or, in terms of derivatives, $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ for $$- 1 < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$0 < x < 2$$ . In other words, the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ . This observation is the basis of the following test.

note.title: The First Derivative Test
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$c$$ is a critical number of a continuous function $$f$$ .

item.paragraph: If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}$$ is positive to the left and right of $$c$$ , or negative to the left and right of $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has no local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ .

subsection.paragraph: The First Derivative Test is a consequence of the I/D Test. In part (a), for instance, because the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$ , $$f$$ is increasing to the left of $$c$$ and decreasing to the right of $$c$$ . It follows that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .
It is easy to remember the First Derivative Test by visualizing diagrams such as those in Figure 4.

note.title: Definition
note.paragraph: If the graph of $$f$$ lies above all of its tangents on an interval $$I$$ , then $$f$$ is called concave upward on $$I$$ . If the graph of $$f$$ lies below all of its tangents on $$I$$ , then $$f$$ is called concave downward on $$I$$ .

note.title: Notation
note.paragraph: We use the abbreviation CU for concave upward and CD for concave downward.

subsection.paragraph: Figure 8 shows the graph of a function that is concave upward (CU) on the intervals $$\left( {b,c} \right)$$ , $$\left( {d,e} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {e,p} \right)$$ and concave downward (CD) on the intervals $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , $$\left( {c,d} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {p,q} \right)$$ .

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick marks a, b, c, d, e, p, and q, in the order from left to right. The curve begins at x = a, goes up and to the right, bends up like an arch, reaches its high point to the left of x = b, and then goes down and to the right. After the curve passes through x = b, it bends down and reaches its low point between x = b and x = c. It then rises through x = c, bends up, reaches its sharp high point at x = d, then bends down, reaches its low point to the right of x = d, then gradually goes up and to the right to a sharp high point at x = e. The curve then goes down and to the right, initially bending down, levels out at x = p, then goes down and to the right, now bending up, and exits the viewing window at x = q. The part of the curve from x = a to x = b is labeled concave down; the part of the curve from x = b to x = c is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = c to x = d is labeled concave down; the part of the curve from x = d to x = e is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = e to x = p is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = p to x = q is labeled concave down.

subsection.paragraph: Let’s see how the second derivative helps determine the intervals of concavity. Looking at Figure 7(a), you can see that, going from left to right, the slope of the tangent increases. This means that the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ is an increasing function and therefore its derivative $$f^{''}$$ is positive. Likewise, in Figure 7(b) the slope of the tangent decreases from left to right, so $$f^{\prime}$$ decreases and therefore $$f^{''}$$ is negative. This reasoning can be reversed and suggests that the following theorem is true. A proof is given in Appendix F with the help of the Mean Value Theorem.

item.paragraph: If $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on an interval $$I$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$I$$ .
If $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on an interval $$I$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$I$$ .

problem.paragraph: Figure 9 shows a population graph for honeybees raised in an apiary. How does the rate of population growth change over time? When is this rate highest? Over what intervals is $$P$$ concave upward or concave downward?

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is labeled Time (in weeks) and is displayed from 0 to 18 in increments of 3 units. The vertical axis P is labeled Number of bees (in thousands) and is displayed from 0 to 80 in increments of 20 units. The curve begins at the origin, goes up and to the right, bends downward until the approximate point (12, 38), then rises, now bends upward, exiting the viewing window at approximately (18, 70).

problem.paragraph: Solution By looking at the slope of the curve as $$t$$ increases, we see that the rate of growth of the population is initially very small, then gets larger until it reaches a maximum at about $$t = 12$$ weeks, and decreases as the population begins to level off. As the population approaches its maximum value of about $$75,000$$ (called the carrying capacity), the rate of growth, $$P^{\prime}(t)$$ , approaches $$0$$ . The curve appears to be concave upward on $$(0,12)$$ and concave downward on $$(12,18)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: In Example 4, the population curve changed from concave upward to concave downward at approximately the point $$(12,38,000)$$ . This point is called an inflection point of the curve. The significance of this point is that the rate of population increase has its maximum value there. In general, an inflection point is a point where a curve changes its direction of concavity.

note.title: Definition
note.paragraph: A point $$P$$ on a curve $$y = f(x)$$ is called an inflection point if $$f$$ is continuous there and the curve changes from concave upward to concave downward or from concave downward to concave upward at $$P$$ .

subsection.paragraph: For instance, in Figure 8, $$B$$ , $$C$$ , $$D$$ , and $$P$$ are the points of inflection. Notice that if a curve has a tangent at a point of inflection, then the curve crosses its tangent there.
In view of the Concavity Test, there is a point of inflection at any point where the function is continuous and the second derivative changes sign.

problem.paragraph: Sketch a possible graph of a function $$f$$ that satisfies the following conditions:

Solution Condition (i) tells us that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ . Condition (ii) says that $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ , and concave downward on $$\left( {- 2,2} \right)$$ . From Condition (iii) we know that the graph of $$f$$ has two horizontal asymptotes: $$y = - 2$$ (to the left) and $$y = 0$$ (to the right).

We first draw the horizontal asymptote $$y = - 2$$ as a dashed line (see Figure 10). We then draw the graph of $$f$$ approaching this asymptote at the far left, increasing to its maximum point at $$x = 1$$ , and decreasing toward the $$x$$-axis at the far right. We also make sure that the graph has inflection points when $$x = - 2$$ and $$2$$ . Notice that we made the curve bend upward for $$x < - 2$$ and $$x > 2$$ , and bend downward when $$x$$ is between $$- 2$$ and $$2$$ .

subsection.title: The Second Derivative Test
subsection.paragraph: Another application of the second derivative is the following test for identifying local maximum and minimum values. It is a consequence of the Concavity Test, and it serves as an alternative to the First Derivative Test.

note.title: The Second Derivative Test
note.paragraph: Suppose $$f^{''}$$ is continuous near $$c$$ .

item.paragraph: If $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ .
If $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .

subsection.paragraph: For instance, part (a) is true because $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ near $$c$$ and so $$f$$ is concave upward near $$c$$ . This means that the graph of $$f$$ lies above its horizontal tangent at $$c$$ and so $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ . (See Figure 11.)

figure.caption: f ″ ( c ) > 0 , f is concave upward
figure.alt_text: A U-shaped curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick mark c. The curve labeled f enters near the y axis, goes down and to the right, reaches its low point at x = c, and then goes up and to the right. A horizontal tangent is drawn below the curve and touches the curve exactly once at a labeled point P and is labeled f prime (c) = 0. The vertical segment from tick mark c reaches the curve at its low point.

subsection.paragraph: Note The Second Derivative Test is inconclusive when $$f^{''}(c) = 0$$ . In other words, at such a point there might be a maximum, there might be a minimum, or there might be neither. This test also fails when $$f^{''}(c)$$ does not exist. In such cases the First Derivative Test must be used. In fact, even when both tests apply, the First Derivative Test is often the easier one to use.

problem.paragraph: Discuss the curve $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ with respect to concavity, points of inflection, and local maxima and minima.
Solution If $$f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ , then

To find the critical numbers we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and obtain $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 3$$ . (Note that $$f^{\prime}$$ is a polynomial and hence defined everywhere.) To use the Second Derivative Test we evaluate $$f^{''}$$ at these critical numbers:

Since $$f^{\prime}(3) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(3) > 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test tells us that $$f(3) = - 27$$ is a local minimum. Because $$f^{''}(0) = 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test gives no information about the critical number $$0$$ . But since $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and also for $$0 < x < 3$$ , the First Derivative Test tells us that $$f$$ does not have a local maximum or minimum at $$0$$ .
Since $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 0$$ or $$2$$ , we divide the real line into intervals with these numbers as endpoints and complete the following chart.

The point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave upward to concave downward there. Also $$\left( {2, - 16} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave downward to concave upward there.
The graph of $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ in Figure 12 supports our conclusions.

subsection.title: Curve Sketching
subsection.paragraph: We now use the information we obtain from the first and second derivatives to sketch the graph of a function.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{1 \slash 3}$$ .
Solution First note that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Calculation of the first two derivatives gives
Use the differentiation rules to check these calculations.
Since $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 4$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 6$$ , the critical numbers are $$0$$ , $$4$$ , and $$6$$ .

To find the local extreme values we use the First Derivative Test. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local minimum. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$4$$ , $$f(4) = 2^{5 \slash 3}$$ is a local maximum. The sign of $$f^{\prime}$$ does not change at $$6$$ , so there is no minimum or maximum there. (The Second Derivative Test could be used at $$4$$ but not at $$0$$ or $$6$$ because $$f^{''}$$ does not exist at either of these numbers.)

Looking at the expression for $$f^{''}(x)$$ and noting that $$x^{4 \slash 3} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we have $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and for $$0 < x < 6$$ and $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for $$x > 6$$ . So $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,6} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {6,\infty} \right)$$ , and the only inflection point is $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ . Using all of the information we gathered about $$f$$ from its first and second derivatives, we sketch the graph in Figure 13. Note that the curve has vertical tangents at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ because $$\left. |{f^{\prime}(x)|}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and as $$\left. x\rightarrow 6 \right.$$ .

It then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, now concave down, reaches the labeled high point (4, 2^(5/3)), then goes down and to the right, and reaches the x axis at (6, 0). After the curve crosses the x axis, it goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant, now concave up.

Solution Notice that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0 \right\}$$ , so we check for vertical asymptotes by computing the left and right limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , we know that $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , so
and this shows that $$x = 0$$ is a vertical asymptote. As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ , we have $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , so
As $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and so
This shows that $$y = 1$$ is a horizontal asymptote (to both the left and right).
Now let’s compute the derivative. The Chain Rule gives

Since $$e^{1 \slash x} > 0$$ and $$x^{2} > 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ , we have $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ . Thus $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . There is no critical number, so the function has no local maximum or minimum. The second derivative is

Since $$e^{1 \slash x} > 0$$ and $$x^{4} > 0$$ , we have $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > - \frac{1}{2}$$ $$\left( {x \neq 0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ when $$x < - \frac{1}{2}$$ . So the curve is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - \frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . The inflection point is $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},e^{- 2}} \right)$$ .

To sketch the graph of $$f$$ we first draw the horizontal asymptote $$y = 1$$ (as a dashed line), together with the parts of the curve near the asymptotes in a preliminary sketch [Figure 14(a)]. These parts reflect the information concerning limits and the fact that $$f$$ is decreasing on both $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . Notice that we have indicated that $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ even though $$f(0)$$ does not exist. In Figure 14(b) we finish the sketch by incorporating the information concerning concavity and the inflection point. In Figure 14(c) we check our work with a computer.

We met some limits of this type in Chapter 2. For rational functions, we can cancel common factors:
In Section 3.3 we used a geometric argument to show that
But these methods do not work for limits such as (1).
Another situation in which a limit is not obvious occurs when we look for a horizontal asymptote of $$F$$ and need to evaluate the limit

It isn’t obvious how to evaluate this limit because both numerator and denominator become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . There is a struggle between numerator and denominator. If the numerator wins, the limit will be $$\infty$$ (the numerator was increasing significantly faster than the denominator); if the denominator wins, the answer will be $$0$$ . Or there may be some compromise, in which case the answer will be some finite positive number.
In general, if we have a limit of the form

We saw in Section 2.6 that this type of limit can be evaluated for certain functions, including rational functions, by dividing numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ that occurs in the denominator. subsection.title: L’Hospital’s Rule
subsection.paragraph: We now introduce a systematic method, known as l’Hospital’s Rule, for the evaluation of indeterminate forms of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or type $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Note 1 L’Hospital’s Rule says that the limit of a quotient of functions is equal to the limit of the quotient of their derivatives, provided that the given conditions are satisfied. It is especially important to verify the conditions regarding the limits of $$f$$ and $$g$$ before using l’Hospital’s Rule.

Note 2 L’Hospital’s Rule is also valid for one-sided limits and for limits at infinity or negative infinity; that is, “$$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ ” can be replaced by any of the symbols $$\left. x\rightarrow a^{+} \right.$$ , $$\left. x\rightarrow a^{-} \right.$$ , $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , or $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .

Note 3 For the special case in which $$f(a) = g(a) = 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, and $$g^{\prime}‍(a) \neq 0$$ , it is easy to see why l’Hospital’s Rule is true. In fact, using the alternative form of the definition of a derivative (2.7.5), we have
It is more difficult to prove the general version of l’Hospital’s Rule. See Appendix F.

Writing $$x = 1 \slash \left( {1 \slash x} \right)$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , so l’Hospital’s Rule gives

subsection.title: Writing Project The Origins of L’Hospital’s Rule
subsection.paragraph: L’Hospital’s Rule was first published in 1696 in the Marquis de l’Hospital’s calculus textbook Analyse des infiniment petits, but the rule was discovered in 1694 by the Swiss mathematician John (Johann) Bernoulli. The explanation is that these two mathematicians had entered into a curious business arrangement whereby the Marquis de l’Hospital bought the rights to Bernoulli’s mathematical discoveries. The details, including a translation of l’Hospital’s letter to Bernoulli proposing the arrangement, can be found in the book by Eves [1].

figure.caption: www.StewartCalculus.com
figure.alt_text: A photo shows the front cover of the book, Analyze Des Infiniment Petits, the Second edition by Marquis de l Hospital.

subsection.paragraph: Write an essay on the historical and mathematical origins of l’Hospital’s Rule. Start by providing brief biographical details of both men (the dictionary edited by Gillispie [2] is a good source) and outline the business deal between them. Then give l’Hospital’s statement of his rule, which is found in Struik’s source book [4] and more briefly in the book of Katz [3]. Notice that l’Hospital and Bernoulli formulated the rule geometrically and gave the answer in terms of differentials. Compare their statement with the version of l’Hospital’s Rule given in Section 4.4 and show that the two statements are essentially the same.

note.title: L’Hospital
note.paragraph: L’Hospital’s Rule is named after a French nobleman, the Marquis de l’Hospital (1661–1704), but was discovered by a Swiss mathematician, John Bernoulli (1667–1748). You might sometimes see l’Hospital spelled as l’Hôpital, but he spelled his own name l’Hospital, as was common in the 17th century. See Exercise 85 for the example that the Marquis used to illustrate his rule. See the project for further historical details.

content.paragraph: So far we have been concerned with some particular aspects of curve sketching: domain, range, and symmetry in Chapter 1; limits, continuity, and asymptotes in Chapter 2; derivatives and tangents in Chapters 2 and 3; and extreme values, intervals of increase and decrease, concavity, points of inflection, and l’Hospital’s Rule in this chapter. It is now time to put all of this information together to sketch graphs that reveal the important features of functions.
You might ask: Why don’t we just use a graphing calculator or computer to graph a curve? Why do we need to use calculus?

It’s true that technology is capable of producing very accurate graphs. But even the best graphing devices have to be used intelligently. It is easy to arrive at a misleading graph, or to miss important details of a curve, when relying solely on technology. (See the topic Graphing Calculators and Computers at https://stewartcalculus.com/_update/media/common/liesmycomp_stu.pdf, especially Examples 1, 3, 4, and 5. See also Section 4.6.) The use of calculus enables us to discover the most interesting aspects of graphs and in many cases to calculate maximum and minimum points and inflection points exactly instead of approximately.

For instance, Figure 1 shows the graph of $$f(x) = 8x^{3} - 21x^{2} + 18x + 2$$ . At first glance it seems reasonable: It has the same shape as cubic curves like $$y = x^{3}$$ , and it appears to have no maximum or minimum point. But if you compute the derivative, you will see that there is a maximum when $$x = 0.75$$ and a minimum when $$x = 1$$ . Indeed, if we zoom in to this portion of the graph, we see that behavior exhibited in Figure 2. Without calculus, we could easily have overlooked it.

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 2 to 4 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from negative 10 to 30 in increments of 10 units. The curve y = 8x^3 minus 21x^2 + 18x + 2 enters the viewing window in the third quadrant at approximately (negative 0.5, negative 10), goes up and to the right through the second quadrant, concave down, crosses the y axis at (0, 2), appears to briefly level it out at approximately (1, 7), then goes up and to the right, now concave up, and exits the viewing window at approximately (2.4, 30).

A magnified image of a curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from 6 to 8 in increments of 1 unit. The curve y = 8x^3 minus 21x^2 + 18x + 2 enters at approximately (0.3, 6), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (0.75, 7.1), then goes down and to the right, now concave up, reaches its low point at (1, 7), and then goes up and to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1.5, 8).

content.paragraph: In the next section we will graph functions by using the interaction between calculus and technology. In this section we draw graphs (by hand) by first considering the following information. A graph produced by a calculator or computer can serve as a check on your work.

subsection.title: Guidelines for Sketching a Curve
subsection.paragraph: The following checklist is intended as a guide to sketching a curve $$y = f(x)$$ by hand. Not every item is relevant to every function. (For instance, a given curve might not have an asymptote or possess symmetry.) But the guidelines provide all the information you need to make a sketch that displays the most important aspects of the function.

item.paragraph: Domain It’s often useful to start by determining the domain $$D$$ of $$f$$ , that is, the set of values of $$x$$ for which $$f(x)$$ is defined.

Intercepts The $$y$$-intercept is $$f(0)$$ and this tells us where the curve intersects the $$y$$-axis. To find the $$x$$-intercepts, we set $$y = 0$$ and solve for $$x$$ . (You can omit this step if the equation is difficult to solve.)

If $$f( - x) = f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ , that is, the equation of the curve is unchanged when $$x$$ is replaced by $$- x$$ , then $$f$$ is an even function and the curve is symmetric about the $$y$$-axis. (See Section 1.1.) This means that our work is cut in half. If we know what the curve looks like for $$x \geqslant 0$$ , then we need only reflect about the $$y$$-axis to obtain the complete curve [see Figure 3(a)]. Here are some examples: $$y = x^{2}$$ , $$y = x^{4}$$ , $$y = |x|$$ , and $$y = \cos x$$ .

figure.alt_text: Two graphs a and b are displayed. In graph a, a curve, which is symmetric about the y axis, is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the second quadrant, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point, goes down and to the right below the x axis, now concave up, reaches its low point in the third quadrant, then goes up and to the right by again crossing the negative x axis, now concave down, and reaches its highest point on the positive y axis. The curve then mirrors its earlier path in the first quadrant. It goes down and to the right in the first quadrant, crosses the positive x axis, now becomes concave up, reaches its low point in the fourth quadrant, then goes up and to the right through the positive x axis, again concave down, and goes down and to the right. In graph b, a curve, which is symmetric about the origin, is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the negative x axis, and reaches its low point in the third quadrant, then goes up and to the right through the origin. After it enters the first quadrant, the curve then becomes concave down, reaches its high point in the first quadrant, and then goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant.

item.paragraph: If $$f( - x) = - f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ , then $$f$$ is an odd function and the curve is symmetric about the origin. Again we can obtain the complete curve if we know what it looks like for $$x \geqslant 0$$ . [Rotate $$180^{{^\circ}}$$ about the origin; see Figure 3(b).] Some simple examples of odd functions are $$y = x$$ , $$y = x^{3}$$ , $$y = 1/x$$ , and $$y = \sin x$$ .

If $$f(x + p) = f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ , where $$p$$ is a positive constant, then $$f$$ is a periodic function and the smallest such number $$p$$ is called the period. For instance, $$y = \sin x$$ has period $$2\pi$$ and $$y = \tan x$$ has period $$\pi$$ . If we know what the graph looks like in an interval of length $$p$$ , then we can use translation to visualize the entire graph (see Figure 4).

figure.caption: Periodic function: translational symmetry
figure.alt_text: A periodic function is graphed on the x y coordinate plane above the x axis. The negative x axis is displayed with a tick mark a minus p. The positive x axis is displayed with tick marks a, a + p, a + 2 p, in the order from left to right at regular intervals. The curve is graphed in such a way that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each maximum and minimum. The curve enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at x = a minus p, then gradually goes up and to the right, falls rapidly, again goes up and to the right, concave down, and reaches its high point on the y axis. It then falls into the first quadrant, concaves up, reaches its low point at x = a, then gradually goes up and to the right, falls rapidly, again goes up and to the right, now concave down, and reaches its high point. The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right and reaches its low points at x = a + p and x = a + 2 p. The horizontal distance between each of the tick marks on the x axis is labeled period p.

item.paragraph: Horizontal Asymptotes. Recall from Section 2.6 that if either $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = L$$ or $$\lim_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = L$$ , then the line $$y = L$$ is a horizontal asymptote of the curve $$y = f(x)$$ . If it turns out that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) = \infty$$ (or $$- \infty$$ ), then we do not have an asymptote to the right, but this fact is still useful information for sketching the curve.
Vertical Asymptotes. Recall from Section 2.2 that the line $$x = a$$ is a vertical asymptote if at least one of the following statements is true:

(For rational functions you can locate the vertical asymptotes by equating the denominator to $$0$$ after canceling any common factors. But for other functions this method does not apply.) Furthermore, in sketching the curve it is useful to know exactly which of the statements in (1) is true. If $$f(a)$$ is not defined but $$a$$ is an endpoint of the domain of $$f$$ , then you should compute $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x)$$ or $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x)$$ , whether or not this limit is infinite.
Slant Asymptotes. These are discussed at the end of this section.

Intervals of Increase or Decrease Use the I/D Test. Compute $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ and find the intervals on which $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive ($$f$$ is increasing) and the intervals on which $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative ($$f$$ is decreasing).

Local Maximum or Minimum Values Find the critical numbers of $$f$$ [the numbers $$c$$ where $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist]. Then use the First Derivative Test. If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at a critical number $$c$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is a local maximum. If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$c$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is a local minimum. Although it is usually preferable to use the First Derivative Test, you can use the Second Derivative Test if $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(c) \neq 0$$ . Then $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ implies that $$f(c)$$ is a local minimum, whereas $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ implies that $$f(c)$$ is a local maximum.

Concavity and Points of Inflection Compute $$f^{''}(x)$$ and use the Concavity Test. The curve is concave upward where $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ and concave downward where $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ . Inflection points occur where the direction of concavity changes.

Sketch the Curve Using the information in items A–G, draw the graph. Sketch the asymptotes as dashed lines. Plot the intercepts, maximum and minimum points, and inflection points. Then make the curve pass through these points, rising and falling according to E, with concavity according to G, and approaching the asymptotes. If additional accuracy is desired near any point, you can compute the value of the derivative there. The tangent indicates the direction in which the curve proceeds.

problem.paragraph: We have shown the curve approaching its horizontal asymptote from above in Figure 5. This is confirmed by the intervals of increase and decrease.
Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x + 1}}$$ .

item.paragraph: there is no horizontal asymptote. Since $$\left. \sqrt{x + 1}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow - 1^{+} \right.$$ and $$f(x)$$ is always positive, we have
and so the line $$x = - 1$$ is a vertical asymptote.

We see that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 0$$ (notice that $$- \frac{4}{3}$$ is not in the domain of $$f$$ ), so the only critical number is $$0$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$- 1 < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > 0$$ , $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and increasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .

Local Maximum or Minimum Values Since $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local (and absolute) minimum by the First Derivative Test.

Note that the denominator is always positive. The numerator is the quadratic $$3x^{2} + 8x + 8$$ , which is always positive because its discriminant is $$b^{2} - 4ac = - 32$$ , which is negative, and the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is positive. Thus $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , which means that $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ and there is no point of inflection.
Sketch the Curve The curve is sketched in Figure 7.

figure.alt_text: A dashed vertical line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The dashed vertical line labeled x = negative 1 is drawn from the second quadrant to the third quadrant, crossing the x axis at (negative 1, 0). The curve y = x^2/(sqrt(x + 1)) enters the second quadrant at the top, very close to the right of x = negative 1, goes down and to the right, veering away from it, concave up, reaches its low point at the origin, and then goes gradually up and to the right, exiting the viewing window at the top right.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = xe^{ x}$$ .

item.paragraph: Asymptotes Because both $$x$$ and $$e^{ x}$$ become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , we have $$\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}xe^{ x} = \infty$$ . As $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , however, $$\left. e^{ x}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and so we have an indeterminate product that requires the use of l’Hospital’s Rule:

paragraph.math: $${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}}_{}xe^{ x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{x}{e^{- x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{- e^{- x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {- e^{ x}} \right) = 0$$

item.paragraph: Thus the $$x$$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

Since $$e^{ x}$$ is always positive, we see that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x + 1 > 0$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x + 1 < 0$$ . So $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ .

Local Maximum or Minimum Values Because $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$x = - 1$$ , $$f( - 1) = {- e}^{- 1} \approx - 0.37$$ is a local (and absolute) minimum.

Since $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ if $$x > - 2$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ if $$x < - 2$$ , $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- 2,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ . The inflection point is $$( - 2, - 2e^{- 2}) \approx ( - 2, - 0.27)$$ .
Sketch the Curve We use this information to sketch the curve in Figure 8.

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve y = x e^x enters the third quadrant very close to and below the x axis, goes down and to the right, initially concave down, then becomes concave up at approximately x = negative 2, reaches the labeled low point at (negative 1, negative 1/e), then goes up and to the right through the origin, and extends into the first quadrant.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{\cos x}{2 + \sin x}$$ .

item.paragraph: Intercepts The $$y$$-intercept is $$f(0) = \frac{1}{2}$$ . The $$x$$-intercepts occur when $$\cos x = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \left( {\pi/2} \right) + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer.

Symmetry $$f$$ is neither even nor odd, but $$f(x + 2\pi) = f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ and so $$f$$ is periodic and has period $$2\pi$$ . Thus, in what follows, we need to consider only $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ and then extend the curve by translation in part H.

paragraph.math: $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)\left( {- \sin x} \right) - \cos x\left( {\cos x} \right)}{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{2}} = - \frac{2\sin x + 1}{\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{2}}$$

item.paragraph: The denominator is always positive, so $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$\left. 2\sin x + 1 < 0\Leftrightarrow\sin x < - \frac{1}{2}\Leftrightarrow 7\pi/6 < x < 11\pi/6 \right.$$ . So $$f$$ is increasing on $$(7\pi/6,11\pi/6)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {0,7\pi/6} \right)$$ and $$\left( {11\pi/6,2\pi} \right)$$ .

Local Maximum or Minimum Values From part E and the First Derivative Test, we see that the local minimum value is $$f(7\pi/6) = - 1/\sqrt{3}$$ and the local maximum value is $$f(11\pi/6) = 1/\sqrt{3}$$ .
Concavity and Points of Inflection If we use the Quotient Rule again and simplify, we get

Because $$\left( {2 + \sin x} \right)^{3} > 0$$ and $$1 - \sin x \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we know that $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$\cos x < 0$$ , that is, $$\pi/2 < x < 3\pi/2$$ . So $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {\pi/2,3\pi/2} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {0,\pi/2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {3\pi/2,2\pi} \right)$$ . The inflection points are $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ and $$(3\pi/2,0)$$ .
Sketch the Curve The graph of the function restricted to $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ is shown in Figure 9. Then we extend it, using periodicity, to arrive at the graph in Figure 10.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of $$y = \ln({4 - x^{2}})$$ .

item.paragraph: Intercepts The $$y$$-intercept is $$f(0) = \ln 4$$ . To find the $$x$$-intercept we set
We know that $$\ln 1 = 0$$ , so we have $$\left. 4 - x^{2} = 1\Rightarrow x^{2} = 3 \right.$$ and therefore the $$x$$-intercepts are $$\pm \sqrt{3}$$ .
Symmetry Since $$f( - x) = f(x)$$ , $$f$$ is even and the curve is symmetric about the $$y$$-axis.

Asymptotes We look for vertical asymptotes at the endpoints of the domain. Since $$\left. 4 - x^{2}\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 2^{-} \right.$$ and also as $$\left. x\rightarrow - 2^{+} \right.$$ , we have
Thus the lines $$x = 2$$ and $$x = - 2$$ are vertical asymptotes.
Since $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$- 2 < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$0 < x < 2$$ , $$f$$ is increasing on $$( - 2,0)$$ and decreasing on $$(0,2)$$ .

Local Maximum or Minimum Values The only critical number is $$x = 0$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = \ln 4$$ is a local maximum by the First Derivative Test.
Since $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for all $$x$$ , the curve is concave downward on $$( - 2,2)$$ and has no inflection point.
Sketch the Curve Using this information, we sketch the curve in Figure 11.

subsection.paragraph: Some curves have asymptotes that are oblique, that is, neither horizontal nor vertical. If

where $$m \neq 0$$ , then the line $$y = mx + b$$ is called a slant asymptote because the vertical distance between the curve $$y = f(x)$$ and the line $$y = mx + b$$ approaches $$0$$ , as in Figure 12. (A similar situation exists if we let $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .) In the case of rational functions, slant asymptotes occur when the degree of the numerator is one more than the degree of the denominator. In such a case the equation of the slant asymptote can be found by long division as in the following example.

content.paragraph: The method we used to sketch curves in the preceding section was a culmination of much of our study of differential calculus. The graph was the final object that we produced. In this section our point of view is completely different. Here we start with a graph produced by a graphing calculator or computer and then we refine it. We use calculus to make sure that we reveal all the important aspects of the curve. And with the use of graphing devices we can tackle curves that would be far too complicated to consider without technology. The theme is the interaction between calculus and technology.

problem.paragraph: Graph the polynomial $$f(x) = 2x^{6} + 3x^{5} + 3x^{3} - 2x^{2}$$ . Use the graphs of $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ to estimate all maximum and minimum points and intervals of concavity.

Solution If we specify a domain but not a range, graphing software will often deduce a suitable range from the values computed. Figure 1 shows a plot that may result if we specify that $$- 5 \leqslant x \leqslant 5$$ . Although this viewing rectangle is useful for showing that the asymptotic behavior (or end behavior) is the same as for $$y = 2x^{6}$$ , it is obviously hiding some finer detail. So we change to the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 3,2} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 50,100} \right\rbrack$$ in Figure 2.

figure.alt_text: A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 5 to 5 and the vertical axis is displayed from negative 1000 to 41,000. The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 5, 19,000), goes down and to the right, concave up, briefly flattens near the origin, and then goes up and to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (5, 40,000).

A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from negative 3 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis is displayed from negative 50 to 100 in increments of 50 units. The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 2.5, 100), goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the x axis at (negative 2, 0), reaches its low point at approximately (negative 1.6, negative 20), then goes up and to the right, and inflects at approximately (negative 1.2, negative 10). After inflection, the curve then rises, now concave down, briefly flattens near the origin where it inflects again, then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, now concave up, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1.8, 100).

problem.paragraph: Most graphing calculators and graphing software allow us to “trace” along a curve and see approximate coordinates of points. (Some also have features to identify the approximate locations of local maximum and minimum points.) Here it appears that there is an absolute minimum value of about $$- 15.33$$ when $$x \approx - 1.62$$ and $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1.62} \right)$$ and increasing on $$\left( {- 1.62,\infty} \right)$$ . Also, there appears to be a horizontal tangent at the origin and inflection points when $$x = 0$$ and when $$x$$ is somewhere between $$- 2$$ and $$- 1$$ .
Now let’s try to confirm these impressions using calculus. We differentiate and get

When we graph $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 3 we see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive when $$x \approx - 1.62$$ ; this confirms (by the First Derivative Test) the minimum value that we found earlier. But, perhaps to our surprise, we also notice that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative when $$x = 0$$ and from negative to positive when $$x \approx 0.35$$ . This means that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$0$$ and a local minimum when $$x \approx 0.35$$ , but these were hidden in Figure 2. Indeed, if we now zoom in toward the origin in Figure 4, we see what we missed before: a local maximum value of $$0$$ when $$x = 0$$ and a local minimum value of about $$- 0.1$$ when $$x \approx 0.35$$ .

The vertical axis is displayed from negative 5 to 20. After inflection, the curve then goes down and to the right through the origin, now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (0.2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1, 20).

The curve y = f(x) enters the viewing window at approximately (negative 0.5, negative 1), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at the origin, then goes down and to the right, inflects at approximately (0.2, negative 0.2). After inflection, the curve then goes down and to the right, now concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (0.4, negative 0.3), then goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (0.5, 0), and exits the viewing window at approximately (0.6, 1).

problem.paragraph: What about concavity and inflection points? From Figures 2, and 4 there appear to be inflection points when $$x$$ is a little to the left of $$- 1$$ and when $$x$$ is a little to the right of $$0$$ . But it’s difficult to determine inflection points from the graph of $$f$$ , so we graph the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ in Figure 5. We see that $$f^{''}$$ changes from positive to negative when $$x \approx - 1.23$$ and from negative to positive when $$x \approx 0.19$$ . So, correct to two decimal places, $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1.23} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0.19,\infty} \right)$$ and concave downward on $$\left( {- 1.23,0.19} \right)$$ . The inflection points are $$\left( {- 1.23, - 10.18} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0.19, - 0.05} \right)$$ .

After inflection, the curve then goes up and to the right, now concave down until (0, negative 4), then goes up and to the right through (0.19, 0), becoming concave up again, and exits the viewing window at approximately (0.4, 10).

problem.paragraph: We have discovered that no single graph reveals all the important features of this polynomial. But Figures 2, and 4, when taken together, do provide an accurate picture.

we see that $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ when $$x > - \frac{9}{7}\left( {x \neq 0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ when $$x < - \frac{9}{7}$$ . Graph the function $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2}\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}}{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}\left( {x - 4} \right)^{4}}$$ .

Solution Drawing on our experience with a rational function in Example 2, let’s start by graphing $$f$$ in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 10,10} \right\rbrack$$ . From Figure 10 we have the feeling that we are going to have to zoom in to see some finer detail and also zoom out to see the larger picture. But, as a guide to intelligent zooming, let’s first take a close look at the expression for $$f(x)$$ . Because of the factors $$\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}$$ and $$\left( {x - 4} \right)^{4}$$ in the denominator, we expect $$x = 2$$ and $$x = 4$$ to be the vertical asymptotes. Indeed
and

figure.alt_text: A curve with two parts is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal and the vertical axes are displayed from negative 10 to 10. The curve y = f(x) appears to run along the negative horizontal axis in this viewing window, passes through the origin, then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, concave up, rising almost parallel to the vertical axis, and exits the viewing window at approximately (1.5, 10). The second part enters the first quadrant at approximately (8, 10), goes down and to the right, concave up, and exits the viewing window at approximately (10, 2).

problem.paragraph: To find the horizontal asymptotes, we divide numerator and denominator by $$x^{6}$$ :
This shows that $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ , so the $$x$$-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

It is also very useful to consider the behavior of the graph near the $$x$$-intercepts using an analysis like that in Example 2.6.12. Since $$x^{2}$$ is positive, $$f(x)$$ does not change sign at $$0$$ and so its graph doesn’t cross the $$x$$-axis at $$0$$ . But, because of the factor $$\left( {x + 1} \right)^{3}$$ , the graph does cross the $$x$$-axis at $$- 1$$ and has a horizontal tangent there. Putting all this information together, but without using derivatives, we see that the curve has to look something like the one in Figure 11.

figure.alt_text: Two dashed vertical lines and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from below negative 1 to beyond 4 in increments of 1 unit. Two dashed vertical lines extend upward in the first quadrant from (2, 0) and (4, 0). The curve has three parts. The first part enters the third quadrant below the x axis, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at approximately x = negative 1.3, then goes up and to the right, briefly levels out at (negative 1, 0) where it inflects. It then goes up and to the right, reaches its high point at approximately x = negative 0.4, goes down and to the right, reaches its low point at the origin, and then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, veering toward x = 2, approaches it. The second part resembles a U-shaped curve and lies between x = 2 and x = 4. It enters to the right of x = 2 at the top, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at x = 3, then goes up and to the right, approaches x = 4. The third part enters to the right of x = 4, goes down, and to the right, concave up, veering away from x = 4, and exits the viewing window above the x axis.

content.paragraph: Our final example is concerned with families of functions. This means that the functions in the family are related to each other by a formula that contains one or more arbitrary constants. Each value of the constant gives rise to a member of the family and the idea is to see how the graph of the function changes as the constant changes.

problem.paragraph: How does the graph of $$f(x) = 1 \slash \left( {x^{2} + 2x + c} \right)$$ vary as $$c$$ varies?
Solution The graphs in Figures 19 and 20 (the special cases $$c = 2$$ and $$c = - 2$$ ) show two very different-looking curves.

problem.paragraph: Before drawing any more graphs, let’s see what members of this family have in common. Since

for any value of $$c$$ , they all have the $$x$$-axis as a horizontal asymptote. A vertical asymptote will occur when $$x^{2} + 2x + c = 0$$ . Solving this quadratic equation, we get $$x = - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - c}$$ . When $$c > 1$$ , there is no vertical asymptote (as in Figure 19). When $$c = 1$$ , the graph has a single vertical asymptote $$x = - 1$$ because
When $$c < 1$$ , there are two vertical asymptotes: $$x = - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - c}$$ (as in Figure 20).
Now we compute the derivative:

This shows that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = - 1$$ (if $$c \neq 1$$ ), $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$x < - 1$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ when $$x > - 1$$ . For $$c \geqslant 1$$ , this means that $$f$$ increases on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and decreases on $$\left( {- 1,\infty} \right)$$ . For $$c > 1$$ , there is an absolute maximum value $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)$$ . For $$c < 1$$ , $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)$$ is a local maximum value and the intervals of increase and decrease are interrupted at the vertical asymptotes.

Figure 21 is a “slide show” displaying five members of the family, all graphed in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {- 5,4} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 2,2} \right\rbrack$$ . As predicted, a transition takes place from two vertical asymptotes to one for $$c = 1$$ , and then to none for $$c > 1$$ . As $$c$$ increases from $$1$$ , we see that the maximum point becomes lower; this is explained by the fact that $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. c\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . As $$c$$ decreases from $$1$$ , the vertical asymptotes become more widely separated because the distance between them is $$2\sqrt{1 - c}$$ , which becomes large as $$\left. c\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ . Again, the maximum point approaches the $$x$$-axis because $$\left. 1 \slash \left( {c - 1} \right)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. c\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .

answer.paragraph: For $$c < 0$$ , there is a loc min that moves toward $$\left( {- 3, - 9} \right)$$ as $$c$$ increases. For $$0 < c < 8$$ , there is a loc min that moves toward $$\left( {- 3, - 9} \right)$$ and a loc max that moves toward the origin as $$c$$ decreases. For all $$c > 0$$ , there is a first-quadrant loc min that moves toward the origin as $$c$$ decreases. $$c = 0$$ is a transitional value that gives the graph of a parabola. For all nonzero $$c$$ , the $$y$$-axis is a VA and there is an IP that moves toward the origin as $$\left. |c|\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ .
For $$c < 0$$ , there is no extreme point and one IP, which decreases along the $$x$$-axis. For $$c > 0$$ , there is no IP, and one minimum point.

For $$c > 0$$ , the maximum and minimum values are always $$\pm \frac{1}{2}$$ , but the extreme points and IPs move closer to the $$y$$-axis as $$c$$ increases. $$c = 0$$ is a transitional value: when $$c$$ is replaced by $$- c$$ , the curve is reflected in the $$x$$-axis.

For $$|c| < 1$$ , the graph has loc max and min values; for $$|c| \geqslant 1$$ it does not. The function increases for $$c \geqslant 1$$ and decreases for $$c \leqslant - 1$$ . As $$c$$ changes, the IPs move vertically but not horizontally.

content.paragraph: The methods we have learned in this chapter for finding extreme values have practical applications in many areas of life: A businessperson wants to minimize costs and maximize profits. A traveler wants to minimize transportation time. Fermat’s Principle in optics states that light follows the path that takes the least time. In this section we solve such problems as maximizing areas, volumes, and profits and minimizing distances, times, and costs.

In solving such practical problems the greatest challenge is often to convert the word problem into a mathematical optimization problem by setting up the function that is to be maximized or minimized. Let’s recall the problem-solving principles discussed in the Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1 and adapt them to this situation:
